explanation: [[kw:Fixed‑rate mortgage]]: interest rate stays the same for the life of the loan; predictable payments (e.g., 30‑year, 15‑year).
[[kw:Adjustable‑rate mortgage (ARM)]]: interest rate may change periodically based on market indexes; lower initial rates but risk of increases.
[[kw:Biweekly mortgage]]: payments made every two weeks (26 half‑payments per year) → loan paid off faster, saving interest.
Other types: graduated‑payment (GPM), interest‑only, reverse mortgage, home equity loans.

confusionCorner.body: The amortization table factor covers principal and interest only. [[imp:Real monthly housing cost includes property taxes, homeowners insurance, and possibly PMI.]]

discoveryHook.scenario: Gary's $200,000 home with 20% down leaves a $160,000 mortgage. To find his monthly payment for a 30‑year loan at 3.5%, we use an [[kw:amortization table]]. The factor per $1,000 is $4.49045. His payment = (160,000 ÷ 1,000) × 4.49045 = 160 × 4.49045 = $718.47. This covers principal and interest only.

teacherCues: Walk through: Loan amount ÷ $1,000, then × table factor.

explanation: The [[kw:amortization table]] shows the monthly payment per $1,000 borrowed for a given interest rate and term.
Steps: 1. Calculate the mortgage amount (purchase price – down payment).
2. Divide the mortgage amount by $1,000 to get the number of $1,000 units.
3. Find the table factor at the intersection of the interest rate (row) and loan term in years (column).
4. Multiply the number of $1,000 units by the factor: $$\text{Monthly Payment} = \frac{\text{Mortgage Amount}}{1{,}000} \times \text{Table Factor}$$.
[[imp:The payment covers principal and interest (P&I); taxes and insurance are separate.]]

notes: Mortgage Amount = Purchase Price – Down Payment.
Table factor depends on interest rate and loan term (years).

blocks.title: 3. Total Interest Cost Over the Life of the Loan

discoveryHook.scenario: Gary's $160,000 mortgage at 3.5% for 30 years costs $718.47 per month. Total payments = 360 × $718.47 = $258,649.20. Total interest = $258,649.20 – $160,000 = $98,649.20. That's more than half the home's value! Long‑term mortgages accumulate staggering interest.

visuals.title: Total Interest: Same Loan Amount, Different Terms (3.5%)
visuals.caption: The 30‑year loan costs over double the interest of the 15‑year loan.

explanation: The [[kw:total interest]] over the life of a mortgage is the difference between the sum of all monthly payments and the original loan amount.
Formula: $$\text{Total Interest} = (\text{Monthly Payment} \times \text{Number of Payments}) - \text{Mortgage Amount}$$.
Even a small reduction in the interest rate can save tens of thousands of dollars over 30 years.
Biweekly payments or extra principal payments dramatically reduce total interest.
[[imp:The longer the term, the more total interest you pay, even if the monthly payment is lower.]]

formulaCard.title: Total Interest Formula
notes: This interest does not include taxes, insurance, or fees.

formulaCard.title: Effect of Extra Payments

explanation: A [[kw:biweekly mortgage]] splits the monthly payment in half and collects it every two weeks, resulting in 26 half‑payments per year (equal to 13 full monthly payments).
The extra full payment each year goes directly to principal reduction.
This accelerates the payoff and significantly reduces total interest.
You can achieve a similar effect by making an extra monthly payment each year on a standard loan.
[[imp:Even small additional principal payments early in the loan can save thousands in interest.]]

formulaCard.title: Mortgage Blueprint Formulas
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Mortgage Amount} = \text{Price} \times (1 - \text{Down Payment \%})$$ $$\text{Monthly Payment} = \frac{\text{Mortgage Amount}}{1{,}000} \times \text{Table Factor}$$ $$\text{Total Interest} = (\text{Payment} \times N) - \text{Mortgage Amount}$$

explanation: Apply the blueprint to mortgage problems:
1. Understand: identify home price, down payment %, mortgage type (30‑yr, 15‑yr, etc.), interest rate.
2. Solve: compute mortgage amount, divide by 1,000, find table factor for the given rate and term, calculate monthly payment, then total interest.
3. Conclude: state the monthly payment (P&I), total interest, and total of all payments.
This approach ensures you don't forget to subtract the down payment or use the wrong factor.
